replies.author: cody-fifth-door
replies.body:
Basically

1. Generate base image with your preferred image model (I use nano-banana-2) on a green or magenta background  
2. Use that as the first frame in your video model  
3. Key out the background color

That's... basically it. I will post a more detailed guide later.

replies.author: Prestigious_Candy968
replies.body: Starting from idle works for generating each clip in isolation, but the original point still stands for transitions. Going from a walk cycle into an attack without a visible pop or reset is the hard part, and that's exactly what would be useful to see.

replies.author: Ok-Role-2536
replies.body: yeah this is the real bottleneck. generating isolated clips on a keyed background is one thing, but seamless transitions between them is where most sprite-from-video workflows fall apart. you'd probably need either crossfade blending in-engine or dedicated transition clips generated from the last frame of one animation into the first frame of the next. would love to see if OP has a solution for that.

replies.author: Prestigious_Candy968
replies.body: crossfade blending is the easier path but it can look muddy if the two poses are too different. dedicated transition clips would look way better but you'd need the video model to reliably start from a specific frame, which is still shaky in practice. maybe a hybrid where you generate a short transition clip and fall back to a quick blend if it fails?

replies.author: Ok-Role-2536
replies.body: the hybrid approach makes a lot of sense. you'd want some kind of pose-distance check before deciding which path to take — if the end frame of one clip and the start frame of the next are already close, a quick blend is fine and saves you the generation cost. it's only the big pose jumps where you really need that dedicated transition clip. the tricky part is defining "close enough" in a way that's reliable across different animation styles.

replies.author: Prestigious_Candy968
replies.body: yeah the threshold problem is real. you could probably get away with something simple like per-joint position delta summed across the skeleton, but that breaks down when the character proportions change between clips or the style exaggerates certain joints. might need to normalize against the skeleton's rest pose first so you're comparing relative motion rather than absolute pixel positions.

replies.author: Ok-Role-2536
replies.body: normalizing against the rest pose is a solid idea — you'd be comparing how far each joint deviates from its neutral position rather than where it is in screen space. one thing to watch though is that even with relative motion, a stylized walk cycle might exaggerate the arms way more than a realistic one, so the delta could still flag as a big jump even when the transition would look fine visually. might need to weight joints by how much they typically contribute to the silhouette, or just clamp the threshold per-joint instead of using a single global cutoff.

replies.author: ThatOtherOneReddit
replies.body:
I'm working on this right now and my solution is animation sequencing where the previous frame from the last animation does a mini animation that goes to the next attack. The issue is at high fps you'll have a much less noticeable cut, but if you purposely cut down the animation frames to like 12 fps you have like 5-6 game frames to make the jump without people noticing.

Also I don't think any sprite game doesn't have some amount of jump cutting it's just if it obviously causes an issue. Cross fade simulating a smear on the transition is an interesting idea though.

replies.author: Ok-Role-2536
replies.body: the 12 fps trick is clever, basically using the lower frame count as natural cover for the transition frames. that's a good point about every sprite game having some jump cutting too — the goal is really just keeping it below the perception threshold rather than eliminating it entirely. have you tried generating the transition clip itself from the last frame to the first frame of the next animation, or are you mostly hand-authoring those in-between frames?

replies.author: ThatOtherOneReddit
replies.body: I'm using a frame from the previous animation (generally the first/last frame that you loop to from idle). My game is a tactics game so right now i'm just doing idle -> attack -> idle. I haven't started trying to do like combo attacks or anything but in theory the same idea would work. If you have solid hitstop in your game and you were doing combo's i'd probably target the first active frame as that is the one most of your hits will transition from since the character would be frozen in that pose before the transition. My demands are a bit weaker than like an action platformer.
